lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Carian, what exactly are you so proud of? And why do you think you deserve better treatment than the rest of us?

lines.speaker: Mausolus
lines.text: My kingship, for one thing, Sinopean. I ruled all Caria. I governed part of Lydia. I brought certain islands under my control. I pushed as far as Miletus, subduing most of Ionia. I was handsome, tall, and steady in war. And above all: in Halicarnassus I have an enormous tomb over me — bigger than any other dead man's, and not merely big, but finished to an astonishing beauty, with horses and men carved in the finest stone, accurate down to the last detail. You would not easily find a temple like it. Do you not think I am right to be proud of all that?

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: So: the kingdom, the looks, and the sheer tonnage of the tomb.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: But, my handsome Mausolus, you no longer have that strength, and you no longer have that appearance. If we appointed a judge of beauty, I cannot say why your skull would be preferred to mine. They are both bald and bare. We show our teeth in the same way. We have both lost our eyes, and our noses have been snapped off.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: As for the tomb, and all those expensive stones — perhaps the people of Halicarnassus can point to them and swagger to visitors: 'Look, we have quite a building.' But you, my excellent fellow, I do not see what enjoyment you get from it. Unless you mean that you carry more weight than the rest of us, being pressed down under stones of that size.

lines.speaker: Mausolus
lines.text: Then all that is no use to me? Mausolus and Diogenes are to have equal standing?

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Not equal, noble sir. No, not at all. Mausolus will groan when he remembers the things above ground, the things he thought made him happy. Diogenes will laugh at him.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And Mausolus will say he has a tomb in Halicarnassus, built for him by Artemisia — his wife and sister. Diogenes, if his body has any tomb at all, does not know about it. He never cared.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: What he has left behind is a report of himself among the best people: the life of a man. That monument, you most servile of Carians, stands higher than yours, and on firmer ground.
